## Statement

The strongest empirical calibration of an unanchored external-control comparison to date is Gupta et al. 2025 (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.2152), which replaced the randomized control arms of 14 oncology trials with external control arms built from a nationwide cancer-center network and benchmarked 15 emulated comparisons against the trials' own randomized results: mean log hazard ratio discrepancy 0.247 unadjusted, 0.139 after adjustment for measured confounders and 0.098 after external adjustment for simulated unmeasured and mismeasured confounders, with per-trial values from -0.229 to 1.205. The bias analysis was prespecified, but the randomized answers were not concealed from the analysts; the trials are named with their published hazard ratios, so this is retrospective benchmarking rather than hidden-truth calibration. No prospectively concealed, analyst-blinded, multi-disease calibration program exists, and concealment is not the only known-truth design, since simulation, open randomized emulation, validation samples and bridge-deletion exercises each quantify specified components of error.

## Why it is open

Residual bias is unobservable in the analysis dataset by construction, so calibration requires settings where a randomized answer exists to compare against, and the individual patient data needed are controlled by sponsors rather than available for an independent benchmark. The one substantial exercise is confined to a single disease area and outcome under unusually favorable conditions, verbatim high adherence, few losses to follow-up and no competing events, so it cannot say how QBA behaves under competing events, poor adherence, heavy loss to follow-up or sparse aggregate data. A benchmark discrepancy is a single aggregate number folding every mechanism together, so it can inform a residual-bias distribution only after sampling error, estimand mismatch and outcome-definition differences are separated out, and whether a calibration obtained in one indication, data source and era transports to the submission at hand is itself unverifiable. Retrospective benchmarking also leaves room for analyst adaptation that prospective concealment would remove.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [Gupta et al. 2025, JAMA Network Open](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.2152) | Retrospective benchmarking study: combines experimental arms from 14 randomized oncology trials with external control arms from a nationwide cancer-center network and compares 15 emulated estimates with the original randomized results before and after prespecified QBA. It did not conceal or blind the randomized control arms. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Extend retrospective randomized-benchmark emulation of the Gupta kind across disease areas, outcomes, data sources and bias mechanisms, and add prospective designs in which the randomized answer is withheld from the analyst so adaptation is removed rather than assumed away, alongside bridge deletion and IPD masking. Publish the exercises as a shared benchmark so competing QBA methods are compared on the same tasks, and pair each calibration with an explicit statement of the setting to which it is claimed to transport. Use the observed discrepancy distributions as priors or stress-test ranges only after random error and estimand mismatch have been separated from systematic discrepancy.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. The strongest such exercise to date replaced the randomized control arms of 14 oncology RCTs with external control arms and benchmarked 15 emulated comparisons against the trials' own randomized results, with the bias analysis prespecified; no prospectively concealed-truth or analyst-blinded calibration programme exists.

**The source titled this.** "Empirical calibration of PAIC and QBA against hidden randomized truth" The title asserts calibration against hidden randomized truth, but the audit found the cited study never concealed or blinded the randomized answers from analysts.

**The source said.** "The only way to measure residual bias in an unanchored comparison is to construct settings where a randomized answer exists but is concealed; the strongest such exercise to date hid the control arms of 14 oncology RCTs and emulated 15 comparisons. No standing programme of hidden-truth calibration, bridge deletion, IPD masking or prospective external-control validation exists, so QBA parameter distributions are elicited with no empirical anchor."

**What was wrong with it.** Both auditors rejected the hidden-truth framing: Gupta et al. 2025 (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.2152) nowhere conceals or blinds the randomized control arms, and describes itself as combining experimental arms from 14 randomized trials with external control arms and then comparing against the original randomized estimates. Its numbers are exact as the entry reported them, but the design property the entry's premise rested on is not one the study had, and GPT-5.6 Sol added that concealment reduces analyst adaptation without being mathematically required for calibration.

Literature and prior-art check
:   **open / overstated.** Retrieved the Gupta et al. 2025 full text (PMID 40136297, PMC11947839). Every number matches exactly: 'we obtained individual-level patient data from 15 experimental arms in 14 randomized trials'; mean log HR difference 0.247 unadjusted, 0.139 adjusted for measured confounders, 0.098 with external adjustment; Table 3 shows per-trial values from -0.229 to 1.205, confirming material variation; and the setting is verbatim 'high adherence to the assigned interventions, few losses to follow-up, and no competing events'. The overstatement is the word 'hid' and the framing 'hidden randomized truth'. Nowhere does the paper describe concealing or blinding the randomized control arms from the analysts; the trials are named in Table 1 with their published HRs, and the design is a benchmarking target-trial emulation in which the randomized control arm is replaced by an ECA and then used as the comparison benchmark. The QBA was prespecified, which is not the same as the truth being withheld. The problem's entire premise (a hidden-truth calibration programme) rests on a design property the cited exercise did not have.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens
:   **open / overstated.** C2-C7 agree with the study details recorded in the repository, but C1 incorrectly calls the Gupta exercise hidden. It was retrospective benchmarking: experimental arms were combined with external controls and compared with the original randomized estimates. The randomized answers were not prospectively concealed or analyst-blinded. More fundamentally, randomized concealed truth is not the only known-truth design. Simulation, openly benchmarked randomized emulations, validation samples, and bridge-deletion exercises can quantify specified components of error, although randomized benchmarks are especially valuable for total causal discrepancy. A collection of benchmark discrepancies can inform a residual-bias distribution only after separating sampling error, estimand mismatch, and outcome-definition differences; it does not identify a transportable bias distribution automatically. Concealment reduces analyst adaptation but is not mathematically required for calibration. The multi-indication standing benchmark remains open and is valuable infrastructure, but it is a roadmap item rather than the only possible validation route. Claims of complete absence in C8 and C13 were not adjudicated as literature-coverage claims.

Decision path
:   `R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)`

:::
